anti_overlap: Leave whether truth-apt-but-not-asserted content (quotation, conditionals, free indirect discourse) counts as a claim to the propositional-content/veridicality lens.
Leave sincerity and dialectical accountability (on the hook to defend regardless of intent) to the commitment/accountability lens — this lens only asks whether an act is assertive in KIND.
decision_lens: Rank the five candidate definitions of 'claim' by whether each tests illocutionary force explicitly (what KIND of act is performed), not just propositional truth-aptness. A candidate fails on its own terms if it would still admit 'which translation' or 'But at what cost' as claims — interrogatives whose content the speaker asks about, not asserts.
focus: Whether the gate's YES/NO test tracks illocutionary force (assertion as a distinct act-type from question, proposal, and expressive) or only propositional-content shape, and where interrogatives with factual presuppositions slip through as claims.
name: fd-pragmatics-illocutionary-force
persona: Apply the perspective of a linguistic pragmatician in the Austin/Searle speech-act tradition (illocutionary force: assertives, directives, commissives, expressives, declaratives), with erotetic semantics — the logic of questions, rhetorical/loaded questions, and presupposition accommodation — as a secondary tool.
review_areas: Whether each definition treats assertion as an act distinct from question/proposal/exclamation, or leaves it to content-shape matching a rhetorical question can equally satisfy.
Whether presupposition accommodation is handled: 'which translation' presupposes a fact the speaker is committed to though the act is asking — do candidates separate presupposed from asked content.
Whether pure expressives ('holy heck', bare 'true') are excluded on illocutionary grounds (no direction-of-fit) vs by few-shot luck — the real gate scored 'holy heck' YES at p=0.731.
Whether the rubric's 'Questions...NO' rule is undermined by having no force-level test, only content-shape shots, so unmatched interrogatives slip through — does any candidate fix this structurally.
Whether proposals ('someone should build...') are excluded as directive acts, and whether a candidate misreads a proposal's embedded justification clause as making the whole utterance assertive.

severity_examples.condition: Flag if a top-5 candidate has this shape, especially if ranked above one that does test force.
severity_examples.scenario: A candidate has no illocutionary-force test at all, only propositional truth-aptness, so it admits essentially all well-formed interrogatives carrying factual presuppositions — not a patchable bug but a wrong target.

severity_examples.condition: This is the current rubric's shape; it fails on ~1,385 real posts containing '?' that scored claim — flag before this ships unchanged.
severity_examples.scenario: A candidate tests force only via surface heuristics ('ends in ?') rather than presupposition structure, still admitting loaded declaratives and rejecting genuine committing questions.

severity_examples.condition: Note as a partial-credit gap even if the candidate ranks well, since the ~34% claim rate traces partly here.

success_hints: Cite the specific illocutionary category (assertive/directive/commissive/expressive/declarative, or interrogative-with-presupposition) for each sampled post, not just 'this seems like a question'.
Phrase any fix as a test applicable to one post ('does the main verb phrase commit the speaker, or perform some other act with truth-apt material embedded'), not abstract speech-act theory.
Cite specific rows from data/gate.jsonl (text, label, prob, mass) for every category claim, matching the brainstorm's own grounding style (e.g. counting '?' posts that scored claim).
task_context: What does 'claim' mean in this pipeline? The gate (src/norvid_studier/gate_prompt.py) sorts 40,943 prefiltered Bluesky posts into claim/nonclaim and has now scored ~33k of them into data/gate.jsonl (each line: uri, label, prob, mass, top_token). Downstream, extract_prompt.py turns each claim into a 'commitment', pairing.py finds candidate contradictory pairs, and tension_prompt.py judges them. The acceptance criterion for the whole system is norvid_studies' words: 'found things I didn't notice but upon juxtaposition oh yeah those cant both be right'. Determine the top 5 candidate DEFINITIONS of 'claim' the gate could be operating on — not five example claims, five rival senses of the word — and rank them by how well each serves that acceptance criterion. Ground every candidate in the ACTUAL scored data: read data/gate.jsonl and data/posts.jsonl, sample real posts at various prob levels, and show which definition each real verdict is consistent with. Known symptoms to explain: questions still score YES despite an explicit NO rule; 'holy heck' scores as a claim; ~34% claim rate is ~10x the design estimate of belief-bearing posts (~3%); the rubric asks for 'asserts something that could be true or false, and that its author could be asked to defend' which conflates at least assertion-vs-question, proposition-vs-speech-act, and defensible-vs-sincere. Read docs/brainstorms/2026-07-29-norvid-studier-brainstorm.md for prior reasoning.
